PIP and Underinsured Motorist Claims in Washington: When the Claim Is Against Your Own Insurer

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·9 min read·November 11, 2026

The driver who hit you on the Maple Street bridge carried the state minimum, and your medical bills passed it before the second surgery was scheduled. Your own insurer has been paying through PIP, and now the adjuster there wants a recorded statement, every medical record back ten years, and an examination by a doctor it chose. It is the same company that has been sending you a renewal notice every six months. Whether it is treating you fairly is measured against a statute and a set of claims rules, and they are not the rules that govern the other driver's insurer.

Third-party claim or first-party claim: what is the difference?

A third-party claim is the one against the at-fault driver, paid by that driver's liability insurer. That insurer's contractual duties run to its own policyholder, not to you, and the claim is settled for a lump sum in exchange for a release.

A first-party claim is one you make under your own policy, as a person the policy covers. PIP and underinsured motorist claims are first-party claims. The Insurance Fair Conduct Act draws the line in its definition: under RCW 48.30.015(4), a "first party claimant" is a person "asserting a right to payment as a covered person under an insurance policy."

The difference shows up in concrete places. WAC 284-30-380(1) and (3) give a first-party claimant a decision within thirty days, or the insurer's reasons for needing more time. When an insurer is negotiating directly with a claimant who has no lawyer, WAC 284-30-380(5) requires written notice before a limitation period or policy time limit may expire, thirty days ahead for a first-party claimant and sixty days ahead for a third-party claimant. And the Act's remedies, covered below, belong only to first-party claimants.

What does PIP pay in Washington?

Personal injury protection is defined benefit coverage, and RCW 48.22.005 spells out each piece. Medical and hospital benefits under subsection (7) cover all reasonable and necessary expenses for care by providers licensed under Title 18 RCW, including prescriptions, prosthetic devices, eyeglasses, ambulance and nursing care, for expenses incurred within three years of the crash. Income continuation under subsection (3) begins fourteen days after the crash and ends when you can reasonably return to your usual work, at fifty-four weeks, or at death, and combined weekly payments from PIP, workers' compensation, disability insurance and other income continuation benefits may not exceed eighty-five percent of your weekly income from work. Loss of services under subsection (6) reimburses what you pay someone outside the household to do work you would have done for it, up to forty dollars a day for up to fifty-two weeks.

RCW 48.22.095 sets the floor an insurer must offer: ten thousand dollars in medical and hospital benefits, a two thousand dollar funeral benefit, ten thousand dollars in income continuation at up to two hundred dollars a week, and five thousand dollars in loss of services. Many policies carry more. The declarations page says which.

PIP reaches more people than the named insured. Under RCW 48.22.005(5), an insured includes resident relatives of the named insured's household, anyone hurt while occupying or using the insured car with permission, and a pedestrian struck by it.

When PIP does not apply

RCW 48.22.090 lists the situations in which an insurer is not required to provide PIP. Most are rare: intentional self-injury, organized racing, war, nuclear material, and use of a car in committing a felony.

Two catch ordinary people. Under subsections (5) and (6), an insurer does not have to cover the named insured or a relative in a vehicle the named insured owns or has for regular use, or a relative in a vehicle that relative owns or has for regular use, if the vehicle is not described on the declarations page of the policy under which the claim is made. A second car insured somewhere else, or a work truck you drive every day, can fall outside the policy you assumed would pay.

How underinsured motorist coverage works

Underinsured motorist coverage pays what the at-fault driver should have paid and could not. RCW 48.22.030(1) defines an underinsured motor vehicle to include one with no applicable liability insurance at all, and one whose total applicable limits are less than the damages you are legally entitled to recover. That second half is the one that matters in a serious injury: a driver can be fully insured to the state minimum and still be underinsured.

Under RCW 48.22.030(3), the coverage is in the same amount as your own liability coverage unless you rejected all or part of it. Rejection must be in writing by a named insured or spouse under subsection (4), but that writing is required only at the original issuance of a policy issued after July 24, 1983, not at renewal or replacement. A rejection signed years ago on an earlier policy can still be the operative one.

Three limits in the same section shape the number. Subsection (5) allows the policy to cap coverage per accident regardless of how many people, claims, vehicles or premiums are involved. Subsection (6) allows a policy to provide that when you have similar coverage under more than one policy, the total cannot exceed the highest applicable limit. And subsection (2) says the required coverage does not apply to umbrella policies or other excess-only coverage, so an umbrella carries underinsured coverage only if it says so.

Hit-and-run and phantom vehicles

RCW 48.22.030(2) extends the coverage to hit-and-run vehicles and to phantom vehicles, which matters when the driver who caused the crash never stopped or never touched you.

A phantom vehicle is one that caused the crash without making contact with you or your car, and subsection (8) sets two conditions. The facts must be corroborated by competent evidence other than the testimony of the insured or anyone else with an underinsured motorist claim from the crash. And the crash must have been reported to the appropriate law enforcement agency within seventy-two hours. The second condition is the one people learn about too late.

Subsection (12) addresses intentional acts. Covered persons are entitled to coverage whether or not the incident was intentionally caused, unless the insurer shows the covered person intended to cause it. If you were the intended victim, subsection (11) requires that the incident be reported to law enforcement and that you cooperate with the investigation.

What does my own insurer owe me?

Chapter 284-30 WAC sets the standards, and its key sections were amended effective October 18, 2026. WAC 284-30-370 requires an insurer to complete its investigation within thirty calendar days of notice of a claim unless it reasonably cannot. If it needs more time, it must tell you why in writing and update you every thirty days, including each item it is still waiting for. WAC 284-30-380(1) requires it to tell a first-party claimant within thirty days whether the claim is accepted or denied, and a denial based on a policy provision, condition or exclusion must be in writing and name the provision. If it needs longer to decide, WAC 284-30-380(3) requires it to say so within the thirty days, give all of its reasons, and keep explaining in writing every thirty days why the claim remains unresolved.

WAC 284-30-350(1) requires an insurer to fully disclose to a first-party claimant all pertinent benefits and coverages under the policy. In practice that is the rule that answers "nobody told me I had that." WAC 284-30-350(7) requires the insurer to tell you in writing if it may seek reimbursement of what it pays, which is how a PIP carrier's claim against your later settlement should first appear.

WAC 284-30-330 lists specific unfair practices, among them misrepresenting facts or policy provisions, refusing to pay without a reasonable investigation, failing to affirm or deny coverage within a reasonable time, forcing a first-party claimant into litigation or arbitration by offering substantially less than is ultimately recovered, and failing to promptly explain the basis for a denial or a compromise offer.

The Insurance Fair Conduct Act and its 20-day notice

Washington voters approved the Insurance Fair Conduct Act in 2007, and its core is RCW 48.30.015. Under subsection (1), a first-party claimant who is unreasonably denied a claim for coverage or payment of benefits may sue in superior court for actual damages plus costs and reasonable attorney fees. Under subsection (2), the court may increase the total award to up to three times actual damages after finding that the insurer acted unreasonably in denying the claim or violated one of the claims rules listed in subsection (5). Subsection (3) requires an award of attorney fees and litigation costs, including expert witness fees, to a prevailing first-party claimant after either finding. RCW 48.30.010(7) separately states the duty: an insurer may not unreasonably deny a claim for coverage or payment of benefits to a first-party claimant.

Before suing, you must give notice. RCW 48.30.015(8)(a) requires written notice of the basis for the claim to both the insurer and the Office of the Insurance Commissioner twenty days before filing. Notice may go by regular, registered or certified mail, and both are deemed to have received it three business days after mailing. If the insurer does not resolve the problem within those twenty days, you may file without further notice, and if the notice is served within the limitation period, the limitation period is tolled during the twenty days.

The Act does not reach everything. Subsection (7) excludes health plans offered by a health carrier, and it protects only first-party claimants, so it is not a remedy against the other driver's liability insurer.

Where this goes wrong

A written rejection of underinsured motorist coverage signed years ago, on a form nobody remembers, turns out to be binding under RCW 48.22.030(4).

A driver runs you off the road without touching you and drives on, and nobody calls law enforcement within seventy-two hours.

The claim against the at-fault driver is settled first, and the underinsured motorist carrier is told afterward. Many policies require notice, or the carrier's consent, before that settlement. Read yours first.

The PIP carrier's reimbursement claim against your settlement is discovered at the closing table rather than planned for from the start.

A lawsuit under RCW 48.30.015 is filed without the twenty-day notice to the insurer and the Insurance Commissioner.

The claimant assumes that because it is their own insurer, the adjuster is on their side. The duties are real, and so is the adjuster's job of testing what is owed.

What a lawyer does here

Reading every policy in the household, along with any old rejection forms, because the coverage is usually the ceiling. Setting up the PIP claim so the benefits are used and the reimbursement claim is anticipated. Getting your own carrier's position on underinsured motorist coverage before the liability claim settles. Holding the insurer to the timelines in chapter 284-30 WAC and keeping a record when it misses them. And, where a claim has been unreasonably denied, giving the twenty-day notice the statute requires and taking the case to superior court if it is not resolved.
